title: The Three Kinds of Memory Tasks
summary: Recall, recognition and relearning: what each asks of memory, why recognition is easier than recall, and why relearning is the most sensitive measure.

lesson.title: Pulling it out yourself
lesson.hook: Why do so many students dread theory papers but relax for objectives? The answer is not laziness. It is a real difference in how memory is being tested.

slides.heading: Three ways to test memory
slides.body:
Psychologists measure memory with three kinds of task: **recall**, **recognition** and **relearning**. Each asks something different of memory, and each can give a different picture of how much you actually know.

This matters for exams too: the same knowledge can look strong on one kind of test and weak on another.

slides.heading: What recall demands
slides.body:
In **recall**, you must **produce** the information yourself by searching memory, with little or no help. Bringing back a classmate's name, reciting a poem, or listing what you were sent to buy are all recall tasks.

Essay and theory questions are recall tasks. That is why they feel harder: nothing on the page hands you the answer.

left.title: Recall
points: Name the three basic memory processes

right.title: Recognition
points: Which is NOT a memory process: encoding, storage, retrieval, relearning?

slides.heading: Retrieval cues
slides.body:
A **retrieval cue** is any stimulus or piece of information that helps bring a memory back. Cues make recall easier.

A fill-in-the-gap with first letters, like 'The three memory processes are e____, s____ and r____', is **cued recall**. The cue does not give the answer, but it narrows the search.

slides.question: A question that gives the first letter of each missing word is an example of:
slides.why: First letters act as retrieval cues, but you still produce the word, so it is cued recall, not recognition.

slides.heading: Why order helps
slides.body:
**Serial recall** is often **easier** than free recall because each item acts as a cue for the next: once you say 'A, B', the 'C' follows.

Research by **Howard (2002)** suggests that in recall tasks, **order associations** hold up better against distraction than **meaningful associations**. A memorised sequence can survive interruptions surprisingly well.

slides.heading: The national anthem
slides.story: Ask Emeka to list words from the national anthem in any order and he struggles after a few. Ask him to sing it from the start and every line flows, each one pulling out the next. He has not learned more; the order itself is doing the remembering.
slides.takeaway: In serial recall, each item cues the next, which can make it easier than free recall.

slides.question: Why is serial recall often easier than free recall?
options: Each item serves as a cue for the next
slides.why: In a fixed sequence, recalling one item helps bring out the next. Serial recall is still recall, not recognition.

slides.heading: Failing recall is not forgetting
slides.body:
You may fail to recall something even with many cues. That does **not** prove the information is gone from long-term memory.

It might be available but **not accessible** right now. A more sensitive task, such as **recognition**, may show the memory is still there.

slides.heading: How your lecturer will ask this
slides.body: Lecturers test the types of recall with scenarios: reciting a poem (serial), listing anything you remember (free), fill-in with first letters (cued). A common trap: calling a fill-in-the-gap with cues 'recognition'. If you must produce the answer, it is recall, however many hints you get.
slides.sampleQuestion: Reciting the alphabet from A to Z is an example of: (a) free recall (b) serial recall (c) recognition (d) relearning
slides.howToAnswer: Answer (b): the items must come out in a set order. In essays, explain why serial recall is often easier: each item cues the next.

points: Three memory tasks: recall, recognition, relearning.
Recall means producing information by searching memory.
Retrieval cues make recall easier (cued recall).
Serial recall is often easier than free recall; order resists distraction.
Failing to recall does not mean the memory is gone.

questions.stem: In which memory task must a person produce information simply by searching memory?
questions.explanation: Recall requires producing information; recognition only requires identifying it.

questions.stem: A retrieval cue is:
options: A stimulus that helps bring back a memory
questions.explanation: Any information that aids retrieval of a memory is a retrieval cue.

questions.stem: Recalling items in a specific order is called:
questions.explanation: Serial recall requires a fixed order, like the alphabet.

questions.stem: Essay examinations mainly test:
questions.explanation: Essays require students to produce information without options to choose from.

questions.stem: Serial recall is often easier than free recall because:
options: Each item acts as a cue for the next
questions.explanation: The chain of order means each item helps retrieve the following one.

questions.stem: According to Howard (2002), in recall tasks order associations are:
options: More resistant to distraction than meaningful associations
questions.explanation: Order associations held up better against distraction than meaning-based ones.

questions.stem: A student is asked to write down every Nigerian state she can remember, in any order. This is:
questions.explanation: Remembering items in any order is free recall.

questions.stem: 'The three memory processes are e____, s____ and r____.' This question tests:
questions.explanation: The first letters are cues, but the student must still produce the words, so it is cued recall.

questions.stem: Tunde cannot remember his old teacher's name even when given her subject and school. Later, he picks it correctly from a list. This shows that:
options: Failure to recall does not mean the information is lost
questions.explanation: The name was in memory but not accessible to recall; recognition revealed it.

questions.stem: All of the following are recall tasks EXCEPT:
options: Choosing the correct answer in a multiple-choice question
Listing items from a shopping list
questions.explanation: Multiple choice presents the answer among options, which is recognition.

questions.stem: Which pair is correctly matched?
options: Serial recall: items in any order
Free recall: items in a fixed order
questions.explanation: Cued recall uses hints to help production. Serial is fixed order; free is any order; identifying familiar items is recognition.

questions.stem: A pharmacist recites the steps for preparing a solution even after being interrupted by a phone call. Howard's finding helps explain this because:
options: Order associations are relatively resistant to distraction
questions.explanation: Sequences held by order associations tend to survive distraction.

questions.stem: I. Recall requires producing information. II. Retrieval cues make recall harder. III. Failing recall proves the memory is gone. Which are correct?
questions.explanation: Only I is correct. Cues make recall easier, and failing recall does not prove the memory is lost.

questions.stem: A researcher finds that students given a list of first letters recall far more words than students given no cues. The best conclusion is that:
options: The uncued students had not stored the words
Some stored words were available but needed cues to be accessed
questions.explanation: Cues improved access to words already stored. It does not show uncued students never stored them.

questions.stem: A student revises by reciting topics in the same order each time, then panics when the exam asks them in a different order. This is most likely because:
options: Serial recall relied on each item cueing the next
questions.explanation: Learning in a fixed sequence makes each item depend on the one before as a cue. Out of order, those cues are missing.

lesson.title: Familiar faces and saved time
lesson.hook: You walk past someone at the market and think, 'I know that face', yet the name will not come. Recognition has beaten recall again. Why is it so much easier?

slides.heading: What recognition asks
slides.body:
**Recognition** asks you only to identify something as **familiar** or as encountered before: a face, a name, a song, an answer.

Multiple-choice, matching and true/false questions are recognition tasks. The key difference from recall: the **correct answer is already in front of you** among other options. You do not supply it; you spot it.

slides.question: Which exam question type is a recognition task?
options: Fill in the blank with no options
slides.why: Matching presents the answers for you to identify, which is recognition. The others require you to produce the answer.

slides.heading: The hippocampus and recognition
slides.body:
Brain-imaging studies show the **hippocampus** plays a large role in recognition, with its activity varying by task. Recognising **famous faces** sets off **widespread activity** in both hemispheres, including prefrontal and temporal areas and the hippocampal region. Recognising **recently seen** faces produces less widespread activity (Henson et al., 2002).

Monkeys with damage limited to the hippocampal region struggle to recognise things they have seen before (Zola et al., 2000; Teng et al., 2000), so this region is essential for normal recognition.

slides.heading: Relearning: the savings method
slides.body:
**Relearning** is the **most sensitive** measure of memory. It was pioneered by **Hermann Ebbinghaus (1885)**, who memorised lists of nonsense syllables and timed how long it took to learn them again later.

Retention is expressed as a **savings score**: the percentage of time saved when relearning compared with the original learning time.

steps.title: Original learning
steps.detail: You take 40 minutes to learn a list of words.

steps.title: Test later
steps.detail: A month later, you cannot recall or recognise a single word.

steps.title: Relearn
steps.detail: You relearn the list in 20 minutes.

steps.title: Calculate
steps.detail: (40 − 20) ÷ 40 × 100 = 50% savings. Half the original effort was saved, so something remained.

slides.question: Original learning took 60 minutes; relearning took 15 minutes. The savings score is:
slides.why: (60 − 15) ÷ 60 × 100 = 75%. Students often wrongly give 25%, which is the relearning time as a share of the original.

slides.heading: Why relearning is most sensitive
slides.body:
Recall and recognition may show **zero** memory when traces are faint. Relearning can still detect a **remnant**: if you relearn faster than you first learned, some memory survived.

That is why sensitivity runs: **relearning** detects the most, then **recognition**, then **recall** the least.

slides.heading: Final exam revision
slides.story: In week one, Fatima spent ten hours learning the topic on neurotransmitters. By exam week, she could hardly recall any of it. Yet revising the same topic took her only three hours. Those seven saved hours were her old learning, quietly waiting.
slides.takeaway: Relearning for comprehensive exams is faster than first learning, showing memory remains even when recall fails.

slides.heading: How your lecturer will ask this
slides.body: Expect a savings-score calculation, so practise the formula: (original − relearning) ÷ original × 100. Also expect 'which is the most sensitive measure of memory' and the recall versus recognition difference. A trap: picking recognition as most sensitive because it is easier. Easier for students is not the same as most sensitive for researchers.
slides.sampleQuestion: It took 50 minutes to learn a list and 10 minutes to relearn it. What is the savings score? (a) 20% (b) 40% (c) 80% (d) 10%
slides.howToAnswer: Answer (c): (50 − 10) ÷ 50 × 100 = 80%. Then state that relearning is the most sensitive measure.

points: Recognition: identify material as familiar; the answer is presented.
The hippocampus is essential for normal recognition.
Relearning is the most sensitive measure of memory.

questions.stem: Which is the most sensitive measure of memory?
questions.explanation: Relearning can detect traces that recall and recognition miss.

questions.stem: Multiple-choice questions are examples of:
questions.explanation: The answer is among the options, so you only need to recognise it.

questions.stem: The relearning method expresses retention as:
options: Percentage of time saved in relearning
questions.explanation: The savings score is the percentage of time saved compared with original learning.

questions.stem: The main difference between recall and recognition is that recognition:
options: Presents the correct answer among other items
questions.explanation: Recognition only needs you to identify the answer when you see it.

questions.stem: The brain region found essential for normal recognition in monkey studies is the:
questions.explanation: Damage limited to the hippocampal region impaired recognition (Teng et al.; Zola et al., 2000).

questions.stem: The savings method was pioneered by:
questions.explanation: Hermann Ebbinghaus (1885) used relearning savings with nonsense syllables.

questions.stem: Learning a poem took 30 minutes; relearning it a month later took 12 minutes. The savings score is:
questions.explanation: (30 − 12) ÷ 30 × 100 = 60%. 40% would be the relearning time as a share of the original.

questions.stem: Ada recognises a classmate's face at a wedding but cannot recall her name. This happens because:
options: Names are stored in implicit memory
questions.explanation: Recognition only needs a sense of familiarity; recall needs the name produced.

questions.stem: A student cannot recall or recognise any words from a list learned a year ago, but relearns it faster than before. This shows:
options: Some memory remained that recall and recognition missed
Recognition is the most sensitive test
questions.explanation: Faster relearning reveals a remnant of memory undetectable by the other tasks.

questions.stem: Henson and colleagues (2002) found that recognising famous faces, compared with recently seen faces, produced:
options: More widespread activity across both hemispheres
questions.explanation: Famous faces triggered widespread activity including prefrontal, temporal and hippocampal regions.

questions.stem: Which ordering from MOST to LEAST sensitive measure of memory is correct?
questions.explanation: Relearning detects the most retained information, then recognition, then recall.

questions.stem: All of the following are recognition tasks EXCEPT:
options: Identifying a suspect in a line-up
Writing a list of all suspects seen
questions.explanation: Writing a list requires producing items, which is recall.

questions.stem: Original learning took 80 minutes. A savings score of 75% means relearning took:
questions.explanation: 75% of 80 is 60 minutes saved, so relearning took 80 − 60 = 20 minutes.

questions.stem: I. Recognition presents the correct answer. II. Relearning can detect memory when recall fails. III. Hippocampal damage leaves recognition normal. Which are correct?
questions.explanation: I and II are correct. III is false: hippocampal damage impairs recognition.

questions.stem: A researcher wants to show that children still retain some of a language they stopped speaking years ago, though they cannot recall or recognise any words. The best method is:
options: Relearning the language and measuring savings
questions.explanation: Relearning is sensitive enough to reveal remnants that recall and recognition miss.
